q: The base hands you the check-in sheet to sign. What do you do before you sign it?
a: Have it added to the check-in sheet
o: Sign — a scratch is too small to matter
Take a photo, but leave the sheet as it is
Mention it at the evening briefing instead
why: Anything not on the check-in sheet may be charged to you at check-out.

fig.title: Check-in at the base
lines: Base staff walk round the boat with you
You find a deep scratch on the bow
It is not on the check-in sheet

q: Your crew is aboard and you are about to leave the base for the first time. What do you do first?
a: Brief them on lifejackets, fire, MOB gear, liferaft and VHF
o: Explain the galley and the heads, then cast off
Hand out the drinks and brief them at lunch
Cast off — the base has briefed everyone already
why: The skipper's safety briefing comes before the lines are let go: where the gear is and how to use it.

q: The lead crew holds a briefing on the quay every morning. What do you take away from it?
a: Route, weather, destination and the harbour plan
o: Only the time of departure — you follow the others
Only the weather — the route is up to you
Nothing — the briefing is optional for skippers
why: The morning briefing gives every skipper the day's route, forecast and berthing plan for the next harbour.

q: It is the last afternoon and the charter agreement says to return the boat with a full tank. What do you do?
a: Fill up at the fuel quay before going back to base
o: Return it as it is — the base fills every boat free
Return it with whatever is left and say nothing
Fill up only if the gauge reads under a quarter
why: Return the boat as agreed: with a full tank, or the base charges for the fuel, often at a high rate.

q: Which of these do you report to the coastguard first, rather than to the lead crew?
a: A crew member unconscious after a fall
o: A blocked toilet at the lunch stop
An engine that will not restart at anchor
A torn genoa on a calm afternoon
why: Danger to life goes to the coastguard first, then the lead crew; breakdowns go to the lead crew.

q: The port police officer is waiting at your stern. Which documents do you hand over?
a: The boat's papers, the crew list and your certificate
o: Only the passports — the boat is the base's affair
Only the charter invoice and the deposit receipt
Nothing — flotilla boats are exempt from checks
why: The skipper carries the boat's papers, the crew list and a valid certificate for port authorities.

fig.title: Port police on the quay
lines: An officer asks for the skipper

q: You are moored stern-to on a busy town quay. Another boat is reversing into the gap beside you. What do you do?
a: Put crew on that side with a fender, ready to take a line
o: Stay below — it is their skipper's job alone
Shout directions to them from your cockpit
Push them off with your feet if they come close
why: Good harbour manners: fend off and take your neighbour's lines; next time it will be you coming in.

q: Your crew opens beers as you leave the lunch stop for a two-hour sail to the evening harbour. What is your rule?
a: No alcohol for you or whoever helms until moored
o: A beer each is fine for everyone, skipper too
No rule — the lead boat watches the flotilla
Anything goes, as long as nobody is seasick
why: The skipper must stay fit to command and the helm alert; the drinks wait until you are safely moored.

q: Your crew wants to visit a famous beach 25 miles outside the flotilla's sailing area. What do you say?
a: No — stay in the agreed area and ask the lead crew for ideas
o: Yes — and tell the lead crew when you get back
Yes — if you leave early and return by dark
Yes — the area is only a suggestion
why: The flotilla's area is part of your charter terms and the lead crew's cover; you stay within it.

q: Your crew asks you to take the boat out anyway. What is your answer?
a: Stay in harbour with the rest of the flotilla
o: Go, but promise to call on the working channel
Go early and be back before the wind arrives
Go if one other skipper agrees to come too
why: Flotilla boats do not sail in conditions above the agreed limits; the lead crew's call stands.

fig.title: Morning briefing
lines: Lead crew: all boats stay in harbour today
Your crew is keen to go

q: On day three you touch the quay while berthing and crack a stanchion base. When do you tell anyone?
a: Tell the lead crew now, and list it at check-out
o: Only at check-out, if the base staff notice it
Never — small damage is covered by the deposit
Only if it gets worse during the week
why: Report damage at once: the lead crew can fix it, it may affect safety, and it goes on the return report.

q: It is blowing force 5 and the sea is rough. One crew member refuses to wear a lifejacket on deck. What do you do?
a: Insist — on deck in these conditions, lifejackets are on
o: Let them decide — they are an adult
Let them, but keep them in the cockpit
Ask the lead crew to talk to them by radio
why: The skipper is responsible for everyone aboard and decides on safety gear; the crew follow.

q: You count the safety gear at check-in. What must be put right before you leave?
a: One more lifejacket — one for every person
o: Nothing — seven is enough for a coastal flotilla
The liferaft — it needs a service first
The flares — they must be renewed every week
why: Every person aboard needs a lifejacket; count them at check-in, before you sign.

q: The lead boat's 17:00 call comes through on the working channel. How do you reply?
a: Answer with your position and expected arrival
o: Stay silent — you will be in within the hour
Call back later on channel 16 instead
Answer only if something is wrong
why: The radio schedule is how the lead crew knows every boat is safe: always answer with position and ETA.

fig.title: Flotilla radio schedule
lines: Lead boat calls all boats at 09:00 and 17:00
17:00 now: you are 5 M from the harbour

q: Your fresh-water pump has failed at a remote anchorage, and the lead boat does not answer on the working channel. What do you do?
a: Phone the lead crew on the number from the briefing
o: Call the coastguard on channel 16 for advice
Send a PAN-PAN so that the lead boat hears it
Fire a flare to attract the lead boat
why: A breakdown with no danger is for the lead crew; if the VHF does not reach, use their mobile number.

q: During your safety briefing, who do you make sure can use the VHF and bring the boat back to a man overboard?
a: At least one other crew member besides you
o: Only you — the radio is the skipper's job
Nobody — the lead boat handles emergencies
Whoever is nearest, once something happens
why: If the skipper is the one overboard or hurt, someone else must be able to call for help and handle the boat.

q: The engine is dead but the boat sails well. How do you handle the rest of the leg?
a: Sail on and call the lead crew to plan your arrival
o: Send a MAYDAY on channel 16 at once
Anchor here and wait for the base engineer
Sail on and say nothing until you arrive
why: No danger, so no distress call; but the lead crew must know, to help you berth or tow you in.

fig.title: Afternoon leg
lines: Wind W 3, sailing well, sea calm

q: Late at night, after a long dinner ashore, your crew want to take the dinghy back to the boat at anchor. Two of them are drunk. What do you decide?
a: A sober driver, lifejackets on, the drunk ones sitting low
o: Let the drunkest drive — it is only 200 metres
Let them swim back — the water is warm
Everyone goes, no lifejackets — it is a calm night
why: Night dinghy trips after drinking are a classic way to lose crew: sober driver, lifejackets, a torch.

q: The lead boat calls on the radio schedule. What do you tell them?
a: ETA about 18:20 — slightly late
o: ETA about 17:30 — in good time
ETA about 18:00 — just in time
ETA about 19:00 — an hour late
why: 14 M ÷ 5 kn = 2.8 h, about 2 h 50: 15:30 + 2:50 ≈ 18:20. Say so, or motor-sail to make it up.

fig.title: Lead crew: all boats in by 18:00

q: Your flotilla is based in Kos. The crew wants to pop across to the Turkish coast, 4 miles away, for lunch at anchor. What do you say?
a: No — you would have to clear out of Greece and into Turkey
o: Yes — a lunch stop at anchor needs no papers
Yes — as long as you fly a Turkish courtesy flag
Yes — as long as nobody goes ashore
why: Crossing a border means customs and immigration clearance both ways, and it is outside the flotilla's area.
